Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 112, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ It is well known that "huwa" (hu) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun of the affair or subject), and its position is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, its predicate being the sentence that follows it. Such a sentence does not have a connecting pronoun (rābiṭ), because it is identical in meaning with the subject. The secret of introducing it with this pronoun is to alert the mind from the outset to the grandeur of its content, together with the added affirmation and confirmation it provides. For a pronoun is understood, from the outset, only as an undefined matter of great significance, so the mind remains expectant of what follows, which will explain it and remove its vagueness; thus, when it arrives, it takes firmer hold.

As for the statement of Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir in Dala'il al-I'jaz that with "inna" (indeed) it has a beauty, indeed that it is not valid without it, this is not accepted. Yes, al-Shihab al-Qasimi said: there is a difficulty here, for if the predicate is taken to be the whole meaning of the sentence, as defined in the chapter on propositions, namely the whole of "Allah" together with the meaning of "one" and the relation between them, then the apparent point is that this whole is not the matter; rather the matter is the content of the sentence, which is a singular thing, namely oneness (waḥdāniyya). And if the content of the sentence, which is singular, is taken, then restricting the absence of a connecting pronoun to the sentence predicated of the pronoun of the matter is not valid, since every such sentence is like that, for the predicate must be identical with the subject in essence, and only the content of the sentence, which is singular, is identical with it in this way. It was answered by choosing the first alternative, as indicated by their sometimes expressing this pronoun as the pronoun of the story (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa), since the content of the sentence which is singular is not a story; rather the story is its meaning as defined in the chapter on propositions. Also, they count as such sentences, which are identical with the subject in meaning and need no pronoun, the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The truest thing that the servant has said, and we are all Your servants: there is none who can withhold what You give, and none who can give what You withhold, and the wealth of the wealthy will not benefit them against You." It is known that one may say that what is said is not the singular content, but the sentence with that meaning. That is why they require the kasra on the hamza of "inna" after "qawl" (saying), and likewise their example for it: "My utterance: Allah is sufficient for me" (nutqī: Allāh ḥasbī wa-kafā), meaning: my spoken words, which I utter with that. For it is evident that what he uttered is the sentence in its well-known sense. The words of Ibn Malik in al-Tashil indicate the intended meaning by his saying that a sentence that needs no connecting pronoun is identical with the subject, namely that it occurs as a predicate of a singular noun whose referent is a sentence, and this is also apparent in what we have said. That this is a matter (sha'n), i.e., something great among affairs, with regard to what it contains, and describing speech as great or its opposite in this sense is widespread and well known.

Al-'Allama Ahmad al-Ghunaymi said: If it is meant that it is identical with it in concept (bi-ḥasab al-mafhūm), then it is problematic, for lack of benefit. If it is meant that it is identical in reference (bi-ḥasab al-muṣaddiq) while the concepts differ, as is the case with all subjects and their predicates, then it may be said that it is also problematic, since the referents of the pronoun of the matter are more general than "Allah is One," and a particular cannot be predicated of the general in universal propositions. The claim of particularity in this context is rejected by their explicit statement that the pronoun of the matter is not free of vagueness. In other words: what the pronoun of the matter refers to is singular, while what the sentence refers to is composite, and nothing singular is composite. That is why they interpret a sentence that is a predicate as a singular term that is true of the subject, so that it may validly be a predicate; and to require this in a sentence predicated of the pronoun of the matter contradicts their explicit statement that it is not interpreted as a singular term even though it occupies its position.

It was answered that the meaning of their saying "it is the pronoun of the matter" is that it is a pronoun referring to it, placed in its position, even though no prior mention has preceded it, to indicate that it is so well known and prominent that every person calls it to mind, every pointer points to it, and every pronoun returns to it. As for their counting, among the pronouns which refer to something later in both wording and rank, the pronoun of the matter, since it refers to the sentence after it, this is a leniency they have adopted, because the explanation of the matter and the specification of what is intended by it is by that sentence; so the referent of the pronoun is exactly the referent of the matter to which it returns. Thus the second alternative is chosen: either "the matter" is intended as a claimed known matter, and the proposition is made personal, like "this is Zayd," or the general meaning is intended, and the proposition is made indefinite (muhmala), being in effect particular, as if it were said: "Part of the matter is: Allah is One."

The vagueness which they are claimed to have stated, namely the non-specification of the part before the sentence is mentioned and its being applied to it, arises. Just as what the matter refers to may be a singular term, it may be a sentence; so let it be the same here. The first alternative is judged to be far-fetched, and the possibility of universality as exaggeration, like "all the game is in the belly of the wild ass," is as you see; so consider this carefully.

They also permitted that "huwa" be the pronoun of the one asked about, or of the one whose attribute or relation is sought. For Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tirmidhi, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, Ibn 'Asim in al-Sunna, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and others, related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, trace for us the lineage of your Lord?" Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ — the surah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Bayhaqi with a hasan chain, and others related from Jabir, who said: "A bedouin came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Trace for us your Lord's lineage. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾," and so on.

In al-Ma'alim, from Ibn 'Abbas: "'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'a came to the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Amir said: To what do you call us, O Muhammad? He said: 'To Allah.' They said: Describe Him to us. Is He of gold, or of silver, or of iron, or of wood? So this surah was revealed. Allah destroyed Arbad with a thunderbolt and 'Amir with plague."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ), among them Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and said: O Muhammad, describe for us the Lord who sent you. So Allah the Exalted revealed the surah."

That the questioners were the Jews is related from al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada and Muqatil, and this is apparent in indicating that the surah is Medinan. It is permissible for the pronoun to refer to that (the one asked about), since it is known from the question, and its mention occurred in it. "Huwa" is the subject, the Great Name (al-ism al-jalil) is its predicate, and "Ahad" is a predicate after a predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for the Great Name, according to the preferred view that an indefinite may substitute for a definite, and that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is One. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the Greatest Name be a substitute for "huwa," with "Ahad" as its predicate.

"Allah," may He be exalted and sanctified, is a proper name (`alam) for the Essence that necessarily exists, as the majority of the Ash'ariyya and others hold, in contrast to the Mu'tazila, who said: a proper name in regard to Him, glorified is He, is impossible, because no one knows His Essence, distinguished by a particularity, so as to be assigned a name for it; rather He is known only through universal concepts restricted to one individual, so the word is assigned to the likes of such universal concepts and is therefore not a proper name. It was answered: He, exalted is He, knows the particularity of His own Essence, so He may assign to it a word specifically, and it becomes a proper name. This is clear according to the view of those who hold that the one who assigns is Allah, the Exalted. But it entails that what is understood from the word "Allah" is other than what it was assigned to, since no one other than Him, exalted is He, knows the particularity of His Essence, which is what the word is assigned to on this view. The claim that the universal concept may be an instrument of assignment while the assigned referent is the particularity that the universal concept applies to, as has been said about this and similar cases, also entails that the word is assigned to what is not understood from it; for we understand from His Names, exalted is He, only those universal concepts. It is evident that the angels, peace be upon them, are likewise, because His Essence, mighty and majestic, is veiled from others, glorified is He. From here some eminent scholars inferred what is reported from Hujjat al-Islam, that the more likely view is that the Great Name functions, in indicating the true existent that combines the attributes of divinity, described with the descriptions of lordship, singly possessing true existence, in the manner of proper names, i.e., and it is not a proper name. What relates to this has passed at the beginning of the book, so refer back to it.

There remains in this context a discussion: personal proper names like Zayd are either each assigned to the specific individual, as is the most common and well-known view, so that when someone is informed of the birth of a son and names him Zayd, for example, without having seen him, this word becomes a name for the mental image that formed in his imagination; and then if the one born does not have this form, the application of the name to him is not according to that assignment; and if it is said that it is assigned to the universal concept restricted to that individual, it is not a proper name, as previously stated. Then, when we hear a proper name of those personal names and have not seen its bearer at all, we do not understand the particularity it has; rather we may imagine it in forms other than its actual form. Or all those empty images are assigned to it, in which case it belongs to the class of homonymous words applying to an unlimited number of meanings. Or the referent is only the particularity it actually has, so that other particularities are outside the referent, and understanding them from it is an error. Then either one abandons the claim that those names are true particulars and says they are assigned to universal concepts restricted to the individual, or one adopts one of the other possibilities; and both alternatives are open to reflection, as you see, so reflect.

As for "Ahad": they said its hamza is substituted from a waw, and its origin is "wahad," and the substitution of an open waw by a hamza is rare, and from it is their saying "imra'a anāt" (a woman who is slow), meaning "wanāt," because it is from "wanā," which is lassitude. This differs from "ahad" (in the negative sense), which is always used with negation and the like. It is intended in the general sense, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then there is none of you who could withhold him from Us﴾ (al-Haqqa 47), and the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Spoils were made lawful for me, and they were not made lawful for anyone before me."

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿Do you perceive any of them?﴾ (Maryam 98), and His words, glorified is He: ﴿So do not call upon anyone along with Allah﴾ (al-Jinn 18), and His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And if one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾ (al-Tawba 6), where its hamza is original. It is also said that the hamza in it is original, like the hamza in the other. The difference between them, al-Raghib said: the one restricted to negation of them is for the comprehensiveness of the class of speakers, and it covers few and many, in the manner of being together or apart, as in: "There is no one (ahad) in the house," meaning: not one, nor two and more, neither together nor apart. For this reason its use in affirmation is not valid, because the negation of two opposites is valid, but their affirmation is not. So if one said: "There is someone (ahad) in the house," it would contain affirmation of a single individual together with affirmation of more than one, together and separately, and that is evidently impossible. And because it covers more than one, it is valid to say: "No one (ahad) of them is superior," and the verse mentioned above is of this kind.

The affirmative usage has three forms. The first is that it is joined to the tens, as in: "eleven" (aḥad 'ashar) and "twenty-one" (aḥad wa-'ishrūn).

Second: it is used as a modifier or as a modified noun, with the meaning of the first (wahid), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for one of you, he will give his lord wine to drink﴾ [Yusuf 12:41], and the saying of the Arabs: "yawm al-ahad", meaning "yawm al-awwal" (the first day). Third: it is used absolutely as a descriptive attribute, and this is used only for the attribute of Allah, exalted is He. Although its root is the same as wahid, ahad is used for other than Him, exalted and glorified is He, as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

*As if my saddle, when the day had declined with us at Dhu al-Jalil, were on a tamed, solitary* [wild ass]

End of quotation. Makki said: the origin of ahad is wahid. They replaced the waw with a hamza, so two alifs came together, because the hamza resembles the alif, so one of them was deleted for lightness. Tha'lab distinguished between ahad and wahid: ahad cannot be the basis for counting from the beginning, so one does not say "ahad and ithnan" as one says "wahid and ithnan", and one does not say "rajul ahad" as one says "rajul wahid". For this reason it is specific to Him, glorified is He. Some also distinguished between them by saying that ahad in negation is explicit in generality, unlike wahid, which admits generality and other than it. So one says "ma fi al-dar ahad" (there is no one in the house), but one does not say "bal ithnan" (but two). It is permissible to say "ma fi al-dar wahid bal ithnan" (there is not one in the house, but two). It is reported from some of the Hanafis that in distinguishing between them he said: ahadiyya (oneness of uniqueness) does not admit partiality or numerical counting in any way, whereas wahidiyya admits them, since one says "mi'a wahida" (one hundred [feminine]) and "alf wahid" (one thousand), but one does not say "mi'a ahad" except "alf ahad". On this is built the question of Imam Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, which he mentioned in al-Jami' al-Kabir: if a man has four wives and says, "By Allah, I will not approach one of you," he becomes a mu'li (one who swears to abstain) from all of them, and he may not approach any one of them except by means of expiation. But if he says, "By Allah, I will not approach any of you [ihdakunna]," he becomes a mu'li only from one of them, and the specification belongs to him.

Al-Khattabi distinguished that ahadiyya is for the singularity of the Essence, and wahidiyya is for negating partnership in attributes. It is reported from the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) that the distinction is the reverse of this. Since, regarding Him, exalted is He, neither of these two matters is free from the other, it is said: "the wahid, the ahad, is in the ruling of one name." Ibn 'Abbas and Abu 'Ubayda interpreted ahad here as wahid, as al-Jawzi said, and this is supported by the reading of al-A'mash: "Say: He is Allah, the One (al-wahid)." It has also been interpreted as that which is not divisible and does not divide. Some eminent scholars said: wahid is predicated of what is under it by gradation (tashkik), so what is meant here, wherever it is used absolutely, is the one characterized by a wahidiyya beyond which it is impossible to be greater or more perfect. It is that which is exalted in essence above all modes of composition and multiplicity, externally and mentally, and above whatever necessitates either of them, such as corporeality, spatiality, sharing in reality and its properties, such as necessary existence, essential power, and perfect wisdom which entails divinity. This is taken from the words of the Chief (al-Ra'is) Abu 'Ali ibn Sina in his tafsir of this glorious surah, where he said: ahad indicates that He, exalted is He, is one from all aspects, and that there is no multiplicity whatsoever there, neither semantic multiplicity, which is the multiplicity of constituents, genera, and differentiae, nor external multiplicity of parts distinguished by intellect, as in matter and form, nor sensible multiplicity, potentially or actually, as in a body. That entails that He, glorified is He, is exalted above genus, differentia, matter, form, accidents, parts, organs, shapes, colors, and all that impairs complete unity and the true simplicity befitting the nobility of His Face, exalted is He. Nothing resembles Him, and nothing is equal to Him, glorified is He.

Ibn 'Aqil al-Hanbali said: what is correct for us to say, along with affirming the attributes, is that He, exalted is He, is one in His divinity (ilahiyya) and nothing else. Others of the later Hanbalis, such as the Hafiz Ibn Rajab, said: He, glorified is He, is one in His divinity and His lordship (rububiyya), so there is no one worshipped and no lord besides Him, exalted is He. After describing Him, exalted is He, with what has been transmitted of His attributes, he chose that what is meant is complete oneness, and this is on both aspects: that the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n), and that it refers to the one asked about. It is not correct that wahid in the numerical sense is meant at all, for otherwise the speech would be devoid of benefit.

Some have mentioned that the glorious name (Allah) indicates all the attributes of perfection, which are the affirmative attributes (al-sifat al-thubutiyya), and these are also called attributes of bounty (sifat al-ikram). And ahad indicates all the attributes of majesty (jalal), which are the negative attributes (al-sifat al-salbiyya). The speech includes that both of these are informative statements about the one asked about being characterized by all the majestic and perfective attributes. It has been objected that divinity (ilahiyya) comprises all of that, and indeed each of the Most Beautiful Names is likewise, because the Essence (huwiyya) is divine, and it cannot be expressed, because of its majesty and greatness, except by saying "He is He." Then this Essence is explained by its necessary consequences, some affirmative and some negative, and the name Allah, exalted is He, encompasses both of them together. So it is an indication of His Essence, exalted is He, and "Allah" is as a definition of it, which is why it is followed by it. The speech of the Chief points to this, and we will indicate it, God willing, exalted is He.

ʿAbd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) and Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) read: "Huwa Allahu ahad" without "qul" (say). They agreed that it is necessary in: ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ [al-Kafirun 109:1], and it is not permissible in "tabbat" (Perish) [al-Masad 111:1]. It has been said: perhaps that is because Surat al-Kafirun is a confrontation with the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or his peaceful disengagement from them, and such a thing is appropriate to come from Allah, exalted is He, because he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is commanded to warn and to strive. Surat "Tabbat" is a rebuke of Abu Lahab, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is of great character and noble manners, so if he were commanded with that, it would require confronting him with it, and he is his paternal uncle, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This surah is tawhid, and it is appropriate that he say it at one time and be commanded to call to it at another time. It has also been said regarding the "qul" in Surat al-Kafirun: it contains what cannot properly come from Allah, exalted is He, such as: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun 109:2], so the word "qul" must be mentioned in it. In this there is consideration, because mentioning it with this wording is not necessary, so understand. Al-Dawani said regarding the omission of "qul" in "Tabbat": it is not far-fetched to say that the statement of rebuke against Abu Lahab, if it comes from Allah, exalted is He, is more effective in restraining him and exposing him. It has also been said: there is in it an allusion that, since he was, despite everything, his paternal uncle, it is not fitting to humiliate him with such words except by the One who created him, for it is not far-fetched that a Muslim might be hurt by his relatives if someone other than Him, exalted and glorified is He, reviled them.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn 'Asakir reported, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "Durra, the daughter of Abu Lahab, passed by a man, and he said: This is the daughter of the enemy of Allah, Abu Lahab. So she turned to him and said: Allah mentioned my father with nobility and honor, and left your father in his ignorance. Then she mentioned that to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; so he gave a sermon and said: 'No Muslim should be harmed by a disbeliever.'"

Then, the affirmation of "qul" in the reading of the majority in the Mushaf, and the commitment to reciting it in this surah and its parallels, along with the fact that it is not the custom of one commanded with "qul" to pronounce in the position of obedience except what is said. Al-Maturidi said in al-Ta'wilat: because the one commanded is not only the one addressed, but every person who is tested with what the one commanded was tested with, so it was affirmed to remain across the ages as a favor upon the servants. It has also been said: it may be said that the one addressed by "qul" is the reciter himself, as if He, exalted is He, informed by it that everyone, at the position of this included matter, should command himself to say it and not to go beyond it. So reflect. And Allah, exalted is He, is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 112, verse 2:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ is a *mubtada'* (subject) and a *khabar* (predicate). It was said that ﴿al-Samad﴾ is a *na't* (qualifier), and the predicate is what follows it, but this is not correct. As for *al-Samad*, Ibn al-Anbari said: There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that it is the lord (*al-sayyid*) above whom there is no one, the one to whom people turn (*yasmudu*) with their needs and affairs. Al-Zajjaj said: It is the one to whom lordship ultimately belongs, and to whom everything turns, that is, everything intends him. They cited (poetry):

*Indeed the bearer of news came early with the best of the Banu Asad, with Amr ibn Mas'ud and with the lord, the Samad.*

And his saying:

*I struck him with a sword, then said to him: Take it, may you be disgraced, for you are the lord, the Samad.*

It is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, that he said: He is the lord who has perfected his lordship, the noble who has perfected his nobility, the great who has perfected his greatness, the forbearing who has perfected his forbearance, the knowing who has perfected his knowledge, the wise who has perfected his wisdom; he is the one who has perfected all kinds of nobility and lordship. It is narrated from Abu Hurayra: He is the one who is independent of everyone, and everyone is in need of him. It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr: He is the one perfect in all his attributes and actions. It is narrated from al-Rabi': He is the one to whom no calamities befall. It is narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan: He is the one in whom there is no defect. It is narrated from Qatada: He is the one who remains after his creation. Similar to this is the saying of Ma'mar: He is the everlasting. And the saying of Murra al-Hamdani: He is the one who does not decay and does not perish. Also from him: He is the one who decides what he wills and does what he wishes; there is no one to reverse his judgment and no one to repel his decree.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abd Allah ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: I do not know it except that he traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "al-Samad is the one who has no hollow (*jawf*)." It is also reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid, and from this is his saying:

*A flame of wars whose steeds never cease, stern, champing the bit, the solid (al-musammad).*

It is narrated from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: al-Samad is the one who has no entrails. This is also a narration from Ibn Abbas. And from Ikrima: He is the one who does not eat. In another narration: the one from whom nothing comes out. From al-Sha'bi: He is the one who neither eats nor drinks. From a group including Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Rabi' ibn Anas: He is the one who neither begets nor is begotten. It seems they made what follows it an explanation of "God." The reliable interpretation is that it means the lord to whom creation turns in their needs and requests. Interpreting it as "the one who has no hollow" and whatever else is other than these two is either a return to them or something the language does not support. The meaning of his being Exalted as lord was taken to be that he is the origin of all things. In the same sense, interpreting it as the absolutely Self-Sufficient, the one in need of whom is everything else. It was said: It is possible that both meanings are intended, so that it becomes a description of him, Exalted, by the combination of negation and affirmation. This is clear regarding the permissibility of using a *mushtarak* (homonym) in both of its meanings, as al-Shafi'i held. The one he preferred is interpreting it as the lord to whom creation turns. It is a verbal form in the sense of a passive participle from *samada*, meaning *qasada* (to intend), so it takes its object directly and with the preposition *lam*. The application of *al-Samad* in the sense of lord to Him, Exalted, is something on which there is no disagreement, though there is disagreement about applying the word *sayyid* itself. The correct view is that it may be applied to Him, Mighty and Majestic, as in the hadith: "The Sayyid is Allah."

Al-Suhayli said: He is not to be described in an idafa (construct) form, so one does not say, for example, "the lord of the angels and of people." The turning of creation to Him, Exalted, in their needs is more general than intentional turning, natural turning, or turning according to the original readiness that is fixed in all quiddities, since they are all directed toward the Origin, Exalted, seeking their perfections from Him, Mighty and Majestic. And the definite article in "al-Samad" is for knowing him, not for anyone else. It was said: because they know his being Samad, Exalted, but not his being One (*ahad*).

This was objected to, saying that it is not free from difficulty, because the addressee's knowledge of the content of the predicate does not require defining it. Rather, it only requires that it not be addressed to him except after treating him as one ignorant, because conveying the necessary consequence of the predicate's benefit is outside this context. So it is better to say that the definite article is for expressing exclusivity (*hasr*), as when you say: Zayd is the man. There is no need for it in the preceding clause, based on the principle that the concept of *ahad*, free from all forms of composition and multiplicity absolutely, up to what was previously mentioned, while they do not know his oneness nor acknowledge it. It was objected that this implies that if the predicate is known to the addressee, it is not stated to him except by treating him as ignorant, or by conveying the necessary consequence of the predicate's benefit, or when exclusivity is intended. This contradicts what is established in the sciences of meaning (*ma'ani*), that the subject and predicate being known does not preclude the sentence from conveying to the hearer an unknown benefit. For what the hearer gains from the sentence is the attribution of one of them to the other and the identity of the one with the other. So it may be said here: they know him, Exalted, in some respect, and they know the meaning of what is intended, whether it is Allah, glorified is He, or something else in their minds. But they do not know that it is He, whether it means the perfect individual or the genus. So Allah, Exalted, specified it for them. It was also said: *Ahad* in other than negation and counting is not applied to anyone other than Him, Exalted, so it did not need to be defined for them. This is unlike *al-Samad*, for its application to others, Mighty and Majestic, occurs in their speech, as in the two verses cited above, and therefore it is known.

Repeating the sublime name rather than using a pronoun was said to be for indicating that whoever is not characterized by being Samad does not deserve divinity. This, as al-Dawani explicitly stated, is derived from the fact that the definiteness of the two components expresses exclusivity. When you say: "the just sultan," it indicates that whoever is not characterized by justice does not deserve sovereignty. It was also said that this is because attaching *al-Samad* to *Allah* indicates the causality of divinity, on the basis that it is originally an attribute, and when Samadiyya is a consequence of divinity, whoever is not characterized by divinity does not deserve it. This was examined, saying that divinity, as it appears, is for Samadiyya, because He is worshipped only because He is the one needed, not vice versa. Unless it is said that what is meant by divinity is its origin and what follows from it, not that He is actually worshipped. He did not limit himself to a single predicate for *ahad*, and *al-Samad* is the sublime name, by saying "Allah, the One, the Samad," to alert that each of the two attributes is independent in specifying the essence. The conjunction is omitted in the mentioned clause because it serves as evidence for it: whoever is self-sufficient in his essence, and everything other than him is in need of him, cannot be other than one, or what is other than him cannot be other than contingent and in need of him. Or because it is like a conclusion from that, based on the principle that oneness entails Samadiyya and absolute independence. In sum, this clause in one respect resembles evidence and in another respect resembles a conclusion, so it is either a new clause or an emphasizing one.

Aban ibn Uthman, Zayd ibn Ali, Nasr ibn Asim, Ibn Sirin, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Sammal, and Abu Amr (and in the narration of Yunus, Mahbub, al-Asma'i, al-Lu'lu'i, and Ubayd) read *ahadun Allah* (without tanwin), dropping the nunation (*tanwin*) because it meets the definite article *lam*. This occurs in Arabic speech, and it is most common in poetry, as in the verse of Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali:

*So I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering Allah except rarely.*

And the saying of another:

*Amr, who crumbled the bread for his guest, while the people of Mecca were in famine and emaciated.*

The better reading is with tanwin, and its kasra is for the meeting of two unvocalized letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*).

﴿He begets not﴾ and so on, in the same manner as what preceded. The negation of this of Him, exalted is He, is because begetting entails the separation of a substance from Him, glorified is He, and that implies a composition that contradicts His being the Self-Sufficient Lord (*samadiyya*, the quality of being the Eternal Refuge) and His absolute Oneness (*ahadiyya*). Or it is because a child is of the same kind as its father, and none is of the same kind as Him, exalted is He, since He is Necessary Existence (*wajib*, that which must exist) and all else is contingent (*mumkin*, that which may or may not exist). Or it is because, as is said, a child is sought by a rational being either for help or to succeed him after his death, whereas He, glorified is He, is Everlasting and Enduring, not in need of any of that.

The restriction to the past tense, rather than saying ﴿He will not beget﴾, is because the verse came as a refutation of those who said that the angels are the daughters of God, glorified is He, or that the Messiah is the son of God, exalted is God above that by a great exaltation. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the continuance of the negation, and the past tense is used to match the words of His, exalted is He: ﴿nor is He begotten﴾, which must be in the past tense. The negation of being begotten of Him, glorified is He, is because it entails substance, and so there would follow a composition that contradicts absolute self-sufficiency and true oneness. Or it is because it entails the prior existence of non-existence, even if only in essence. Or it is because it entails a homogeneity that is impossible for the Necessary Existent. He placed the negation of begetting first because it is the more important, since a group of the disbelievers imagined the opposite of it, unlike the negation of being begotten. Or it is because those who imagine the opposite of the first are more numerous than those who imagine the opposite of the second, on the basis that the Christians, by way of their claim of incarnation (*ittihad*), are necessarily committed to saying that begetting and being begotten apply to the one they believe to be God.

That is in accordance with what their books contain: they say that the Father is the first *uqnum* (hypostasis) of the Trinity, and the Son is the second, who proceeds from Him by an eternal procession, equal to Him in eternity, and the Holy Spirit is the third, who proceeds from both of them in the same way. The divine nature is one, and it belongs to each of the three, and each of them is united with it. Yet they are three substances, not one substance. The Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, and they (the Father and the Son) are not the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless they are one God, since they have one divinity (*lahut*), one nature, and one substance, and each of them is united with the divinity, although there is a distinction among them. The first is the Necessary Existence of the substance; the second is the substantial intellect, called the Word; and the third is the substantial will, called the Love. Thus God is three substantial hypostases, and they, with their true distinction, are sometimes called by a relative (*idafi*) distinction, that is, by the relation of some of them to others, of one substance and one nature, which is God, and there is nothing in Him other than that. Rather, everything that is within Him is the very essence of Him. They say that in Him, exalted is He above what they say, there are four relations: the first is the active [relation] of intellection in the first hypostasis; the second is the passive [relation] of being intellected in the second hypostasis, which is the image of the intellect of the Father; the third is the active [relation] of emanation in the first and second hypostases, which have the will; and the fourth is the passive [relation] of this emanation in the third hypostasis, which is the love of the divine will that belongs to the first and second hypostases. They claim that the expression of activity and passivity regarding the divine hypostases is used in a figurative sense, and the activity of the Father toward the Son is nothing but the fatherhood, and in Him and in the Son toward the Holy Spirit it is nothing but the beginning of its procession from them both. The passivity in the Son and the Holy Spirit is nothing but the sonship in the Son and the procession in the Spirit. They say that all of that is among the things that must be believed, even if it is beyond the human level. They allege that these hypostases have names which they received from the disciples. The first hypostasis in the divine nature is called Father, the second Son, Word, Wisdom, Light, Radiance and Ray, and the third the Holy Spirit and *Mughri* (the Paraclete), and this is the meaning of their saying in Greek: *Araclit* (Paraclete). In explaining the reason for the designation, they said: this is because the first hypostasis is like a spring and a source, which gave the second hypostasis that proceeds from it, by an act that implies a likeness to its agent, namely the act of intellect, its nature and its whole substance, so that the second hypostasis, which is the divine substantial image of the first, is equal to it in the fullest equality. The definition of begetting is the emanation of a living being from a living being through an instrument and a concomitant source that implies a likeness of nature. Here it is the same, but even more so, because the second possesses the divine nature itself. So there is no wonder if the first is called Father and the second Son. The second is called Word because begetting is not like the begetting of animals and plants; rather, intellect acts, that is, the Father conceives His divinity and understands His essence, and there is no doubt that that image is a word, since it is the conceptual content of the intellect and its utterance. It is called Wisdom because it was begotten of the Father by the act of His divine intellect, which is wisdom. It is called light, ray and radiance because, since it is wisdom, through it is the knowledge and disclosure of the realities of things, as has been mentioned. The third is called Holy Spirit because it proceeds from the Father and the Son by the act of will, which is one for the Father and the Son, and it issues forth from them both by an act like the stirring of the will with love toward its beloved. Therefore it is the love of God, and God Himself is pure spirit, and holiness is His very essence. Each of the first and second has a claim to be called spirit, because of their union. But since the first was called by a name that indicates its rank and its relation to the second, and the second likewise, the third was singled out for the common name and was not called Son, even though it has the nature and substance of the Father just as the Son does, because it did not proceed from the Father by an act that implies a likeness to its agent, that is to say by the act of intellect, but rather proceeded from Him by the act of will. So the second from the first is like Abel from Adam, and the third is like Eve from him, and all are one reality. Yet Abel is called son, and Eve is not called daughter. It is said that the third is called *maghza* (the one sent forth), because he was ready to come to the disciples and make them rejoice (*yughrih*), for the loss of the Messiah, peace be upon him. As for activity and passivity, they are not actually existent in the case of these hypostases, and fatherhood and sonship here do not imply them, as they do in created things. For this reason, here one does not say that the Father is the cause and reason of His Son, although that is said there (in created things). The three are equal in substance, essence, the deserving of worship, and excellence in every respect.

Then they claimed the incarnation of the second hypostasis, which is the Word, and its union with the most noble parts of the Virgin's blood by the power of the Holy Spirit. Thus the Messiah, peace be upon him, was composed of humanity (*nasut*) and the Word. The Word, despite its union, did not depart from its simplicity and was not changed, because it is the limit to which the union reaches. So there is no impediment on its side to the union, and likewise there is no impediment on the side of humanity. Nothing is beyond God's power. They claimed that the Messiah, peace be upon him, was perfect God and perfect man, with two natures and two wills, subsisting in a divine hypostasis, which is the hypostasis of the Word. Therefore the divine and human attributes are predicated of him together, but from two different aspects.

Then they added another note to the lute and said: One day the Messiah fed the disciples bread and gave them wine to drink, and said: "You have eaten my flesh and drunk my blood, so you have become united with me, and I am united with the Father." And there are other such fancies, too well known to be mentioned.

From what we have mentioned it is known that for them there is no difference between saying that God, exalted is He, is the Messiah, and saying that the Messiah is His son, and saying that He, glorified is He, is the third of three. For this reason each of these sayings was ascribed to them in the revelation, and there is no need to make each saying belong to a particular group among them, as more than one of the exegetes and theologians has said. Furthermore, the contradiction of what they have mentioned with the Oneness and the Self-Sufficiency is not hidden. Their saying that the hypostases, despite being three distinct substances with a true distinction, are one substance, is manifestly false, and so it neither fattens nor satisfies.

The example they give to clarify this is far from clarifying, and is a thousand thousand stations removed from the intended meaning. We had mentioned within this book what relates to some of their beliefs along with a refutation of them, but that was before we examined their books, and in it we relied on what the theologians reported about them. Today we are resolved to compose a treatise containing a precise statement of their beliefs about the Necessary Existent, exalted is He, and a mention of their rational and transmitted doubts on which they rely and which they depend upon for the doctrine of the Trinity, as we have found them in their books, along with a refutation of these in the most complete manner, God willing. We ask God, exalted is He, for success in that, and that He, glorified is He, guide us in all our affairs on the straightest paths. For He, glorified is He, is the Most Generous, the most generous, who never rebuffs one who turns to Him.

Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, on surah 112, verse 4:

﴿And there is none comparable to Him, any one.﴾ That is: no one is equal to Him, none is like Him, and none is suited to Him, whether a spouse or otherwise. It has been said that it is a negation of the equality (kafa'a) that is considered between spouses, and it is as you see.

"Lahu" (لَهُ) is a complement (ṣila) of "kufuwan" (كُفُوًا), according to what al-Mubarrad and others held. The original order would be for it to come later, but it was placed first for emphasis, because the intended meaning is the negation of equality from His own essence, exalted and majestic is He. Also for emphasis, the predicate was placed first, together with what that involves of observing the verse-endings (fawasil). It has been said to him that the adverbial phrase here, even though it is not a complete predicate, would invalidate the meaning if it were dropped, because if you said "lam yakun kufuwan ahad" ("there was not any equal one"), it would have no meaning. So when it was needed, it took the place of a predicate, and that was good. Abu Hayyan said: Sibawayh's statement concerns the adverbial phrase that can be a predicate, which is the complete adverbial phrase, and what is here is not like that. Ibn al-Hajib said: the adverbial phrase was placed first for the verse-endings and observing them, and it was not placed before "ahad" so that the subject and its predicate would not be separated; and in this there is a clear objection. It is also permitted that the adverbial phrase be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "ahad," placed before it for the sake of the verse-ending and so that it would not be confused with an attribute or a complement; and that it be the predicate of "yakun"; and "kufuwan" would be a circumstantial clause of "ahad," placed before it because it is an indefinite noun; or a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in the adverbial phrase that occurs as the predicate. This last view was transmitted by Abu Ali in al-Hujja from some grammarians, and it was rejected on the ground that, as you have just heard from Abu Hayyan, it is an incomplete adverbial phrase that cannot validly be a predicate. If a specific complement is assumed for it, such as "mumāthil" (equal to) or something similar by which the meaning is completed, then "kufuwan" would be an extra element.

It may be that the three sentences were joined by conjunction, and no others of this surah were, because they were brought for one meaning and one purpose, which is the negation of likeness and correspondence from Him, exalted is He, in any respect, and what their divisions contain. For the like is either a child, or a parent, or the counterpart of one of these two. Because the divisions differ while being gathered in the thing divided, the conjunction with "wa" (and) became necessary, as the rules of the science of meanings (ma'ani) require. In "kufuwan" there are dialect forms: the kaf with a damma, with a kasra, and with a fatha, with the fa' sukun, and the kaf with a damma and the fa' with a damma. Hamza, Ya'qub, and Nafi' in one transmission read "kufu'an" with hamza and lightening, and Hafs read with the vowel and replacing the hamza with a waw, and the rest of the seven read with the vowel with hamza. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi' in one transmission made the hamza easier, and in another transmission from him it is "kufan" without hamza: he moved the vowel of the hamza to the fa' and dropped the hamza. Sulayman ibn Ali ibn Abd Allah ibn Abbas read "kifa'" with a kasra on the kaf, a fatha on the fa', and the long vowel, as in the words of al-Nabigha:

"Do not hurl me with a pillar that has no equal."

That is: no one like it, as al-A'lam said. This glorious surah, despite the shortness of its extent, comprises a range of divine knowledge and Islamic beliefs; therefore there came in it what came of reports, and what came of traditions, and it indicates the realisation of the meaning of divinity (uluhiyya) through self-sufficiency (samadiyya), whose meaning is necessary existence (wujub al-wujud), or being the origin (mabda'iyya) of the existence of everything else among existents. Then it followed this with an explanation that nothing else is generated from Him, because He is not generated from anything else. It made clear that He, exalted is He, though He is god to all existents and the bestower of existence upon them, it is not permissible that He bestow existence upon the like of Himself, just as His existence was not from anything else. Then it followed this with an explanation that there is nothing in existence that equals Him in strength of existence. So from the beginning of the surah to "al-Samad" is an explanation of His quiddity, exalted is He, and the necessary attributes of His quiddity, and the unity of His reality, and that He is not composite at all. And from His words, exalted is He, "He does not beget" to "any one" is an explanation that there is nothing equal to Him in His kind nor in His genus, neither by His being generated, nor by His being that from which something is generated, nor by His being matched in existence. By this extent the complete knowledge of His essence, exalted and majestic is He, is attained. End.

It indicated in it that "wa lam yulad" (and He was not begotten) is like a justification for what precedes it, as if it had said before: everything that is material, or has a connection with matter, is generated from something else; so the sense of the statement becomes: "He does not beget, because He was not generated." The indication of its proof is in "huwa" (He) at the beginning of the surah, for since He has no quiddity and no consideration apart from His being He in His essence, it is necessary that He not be generated from another, otherwise His identity would be derived from another, and so He would not be He in His essence. The apparent conjunction requires that what he indicated of causality not be considered; and you have learned earlier the reason for its mention. Some have made the conjunction in it close to the conjunction in "la yasta'khirun" over "la yasta'qimun" (they cannot precede / they cannot delay). Some of the early scholars indicated that the mention of that is because it came in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul): they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about his Lord, exalted is He, "of what is He? Is He of such or of such? And from whom did He inherit the world, and to whom will He bequeath it?" The Imam said: "Huwa Allah" is one of three expressions, and each of them is an indication of a station of the seekers. The first station is the station of those brought near, and it is the highest of the stations of those travelling to God, exalted is He. These looked with the eyes of their intellects at the quiddities of things and their realities as such, and they saw no existent except the Real, because He is the one whose existence is necessary in Himself, and everything else is possible in itself, so in respect of its own essence it is nonexistent. So they said: "Huwa" is an indication of the Real, since in their view there is no existent that returns to Him other than Him, exalted and majestic, so that it would need distinguishing. The second station belongs to the people of the right hand. These witnessed the Real, glorified is He, as existent, and likewise witnessed creation, so multiplicity arose among existents in their view, and so "huwa" was not sufficient to indicate the Real, but a distinguisher was necessary; so they needed to join the word "Allah" to another word, and so it was said for their sake: "Huwa Allah."

The third station is the station of the people of the left hand, who permit that the Necessary Existent be more than one, and the god is likewise; so "ahad" (one) came as a refutation of them and an annulment of their saying. End.

Some of the Sufis counted the word "huwa" among the Most Beautiful Names. Rather, one of them said that the letter of absence (ha' al-ghayba) is His true name, exalted is He, because it indicates absolute identity, together with being one of the necessities of breathing by which the life of the soul continues, and the drawing of its trace through encompassment, and its rank in number toward its permanence and non-annihilation. Al-Dawani transmitted from the Imam that he said: "Some shaykhs taught me: 'O Huwa, O He who is He, O He than whom there is no god but He.'" And upon this is the belief of most shaykhs today. This is not found in the reports accepted by the traditionists (muhaddithun). And God, exalted is He, knows best.
